entry.title: Infinix Hot 60i Review: The NFC Budget Phone That Actually Makes Sense
entry.summary: NFC is one of those features that budget phones usually skip. It is expensive to licence, rarely advertised in this price bracket, and most buyers do not know they want it until they try to use it. The Infinix Hot 60i includes it anyway, and…
entry.content:
NFC is one of those features that budget phones usually skip. It is expensive to licence, rarely advertised in this price bracket, and most buyers do not know they want it until they try to use it. The Infinix Hot 60i includes it anyway, and in Kenya in 2026, that decision looks smarter than Infinix probably intended.

Safaricom and Pesapal have been rolling out Tap-to-Pay across merchant outlets in Kenya, allowing customers with NFC-enabled phones to tap on a POS terminal and complete an M-Pesa payment without entering a Till number . This is not a future concept. It is live at Java House, Artcaffé, and thousands of other retail outlets already using Pesapal terminals . A budget phone with NFC is no longer a novelty. It is a practical advantage.

But NFC alone does not make a phone worth buying. The Hot 60i has real strengths and real compromises. Here is what you actually get.

What the KES 14,899 Configuration Offers

The Hot 60i is sold in several configurations in Kenya, and the pricing is inconsistent. Jumia lists a 6GB/128GB model at KES 14,899 , while another listing shows an 8GB/256GB variant at KES 19,750 . A separate seller lists a 6GB/128GB unit at KES 23,500, which is clearly overpriced for this bracket . For the sub-15K buyer, the Jumia 6GB/128GB listing is the relevant model.

The processor is a MediaTek Helio G81 Ultimate, paired with Android 15 and Infinix's XOS 15.1 skin . The battery is 5,160mAh, and some listings claim 45W fast charging, though this figure varies by region and seller . The display is a 6.7-inch panel, and here the listings disagree sharply. Some sources list it as 720p , while one Jumia listing claims 1080x2460 FHD+ . You should confirm the resolution with the seller before paying, because the difference is significant.

The camera setup is a 50MP main sensor paired with a 2MP secondary lens, and an 8MP selfie camera . There is a side-mounted fingerprint sensor, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and stereo speakers . The microSD situation is also unclear across listings, so verify expandability if you need it.

The NFC Advantage in Kenya

This is the headline feature, and it deserves proper context.

M-Pesa Tap-to-Pay works by tapping an NFC-enabled phone on an NFC-enabled POS terminal, verifying the transaction details, and entering your M-Pesa PIN . It reduces queues, cuts down on wrong Till number entries, and speeds up checkout. For a Kenyan buyer who frequents supermarkets, coffee shops, or any merchant with a Pesapal terminal, this is a genuinely useful feature that most sub-15K phones do not offer.

The catch is that Tap-to-Pay is not universal yet. It works only at merchants with enabled POS devices, and the rollout is expanding but not complete . If you shop mostly at informal traders, kiosks, or matatu stages, you will not use NFC often. But if you live in Nairobi and pay at established retailers, the convenience is real.

The Compromises You Will Feel

The display is the biggest concern. If the Kenyan units are indeed 720p, text and images will look soft on a 6.7-inch screen. This is the standard trade-off in this bracket, but it is worth confirming before purchase because the listing information is contradictory.

The second compromise is storage speed. The Hot 60i uses eMMC 5.1 storage, which is slower than the UFS technology found in slightly more expensive phones . App launches and file transfers will feel slower than they should, especially if you are used to a faster device.

The third compromise is performance. The Helio G81 Ultimate is an entry-level chip. Benchmark results show a 3DMark Wild Life score of 648, with graphics tests running at roughly 4 frames per second . WhatsApp, M-Pesa, and browsing will work. Gaming and heavy multitasking will not. This is a phone for the basics.

The Verdict

Buy the Infinix Hot 60i if: you want NFC for M-Pesa Tap-to-Pay at a budget price, you need a large screen and a reliable battery for daily use, and you accept that this is a device for communication and light browsing rather than performance. The 6GB/128GB model at KES 14,899 is the version to target.

Skip it if: you can stretch to the Samsung Galaxy A07 for its six-year update promise, you need a confirmed sharp display and cannot verify the resolution before buying, or you rarely shop at merchants with NFC terminals. In those cases, the NFC advantage disappears, and the Hot 60i becomes an ordinary budget phone with an uncertain spec sheet.

The Infinix Hot 60i is not the best phone under KES 15,000 on raw performance. But it is the only one that anticipates how Kenyans will pay for things in the next few years. That makes it worth considering, provided you confirm exactly what you are buying.

Quick Verdict Card

Buy it if Skip it if
You want NFC for M-Pesa Tap-to-Pay at a budget price You cannot confirm the display resolution before buying
You need 6GB RAM and 128GB storage under KES 15,000 You want guaranteed long-term software updates (Samsung wins)
You shop regularly at Pesapal-enabled retailers You mostly buy from informal traders without NFC terminals

Value Score: 3 / 5 — The NFC feature is genuinely useful for urban Kenyan buyers, but the inconsistent spec listings and slow storage keep it from a higher score.

entry.title: The Real Cost of "Cheap" Data: How Safaricom's B-Live Changes Are Hurting Small Buyers
entry.summary: Samuel Waititu posted a complaint on Safaricom's social feed on 10 August 2026. The one-hour bundle was gone. B-Live was unavailable. Safaricom replied the same day that it was sorry and had taken his feedback. It did not say whether the product had been withdrawn,…
entry.content:
Samuel Waititu posted a complaint on Safaricom's social feed on 10 August 2026. The one-hour bundle was gone. B-Live was unavailable. Safaricom replied the same day that it was sorry and had taken his feedback. It did not say whether the product had been withdrawn, restricted, or repriced .

The silence was the answer. Within days, Safaricom confirmed the new reality. Only one B-Live offering would remain: KES 25, available daily between 23:00 and 16:00 . The hours between 16:00 and 23:00, the exact window when a boda rider finishes a shift, a student opens a laptop, and a trader posts stock to WhatsApp Status, were no longer covered.

No price was raised. The shilling figure on the menu did not change. But the product that made data affordable for millions of Kenyans was quietly removed, and the effective cost of getting online for an afternoon rose by half.

What B-Live Was, and What It Became

B-Live was built for people who could not pre-commit KES 1,000 for a monthly bundle. It sold time instead of volume. KES 20 bought an hour. KES 50 bought three hours. KES 150 bought six . For a trader with KES 50 in M-Pesa and an uncertain day ahead, that was the only way to get online at all.

The new structure is different. The KES 20 hourly option is gone. What remains is KES 25 for one hour, plus ten voice minutes, available only outside the evening peak . The hourly price rose 25 per cent. The multi-hour blocks that let someone plan an afternoon online disappeared. The effective cost of that afternoon rose from KES 16.67 an hour to KES 25, an increase of 50 per cent .

And the seven hours between 16:00 and 23:00? No B-Live access at all.

Who This Hurts, and Why the Numbers Prove It

The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics recorded 18.1 million people in informal employment in 2025, against 3.31 million in formal wage employment. That is 83.8 per cent of all jobs . These workers are paid when a fare is completed or a harvest sells. They do not have a salary date. They cannot pre-commit KES 1,000 for thirty days, no matter how good the per-gigabyte price looks on paper.

The Communications Authority estimates average data use at about 5GB a month per subscription. Safaricom's own audited figure is 4.92GB. But the average hides a split. Roughly half of Safaricom's mobile data subscribers use less than 1GB in a month . For that half, the hourly bundle was not a marginal product. It was the entire product. Safaricom's chief financial officer described these customers as a "large opportunity" .

Removing the product they rely on is not a pricing adjustment. It is removing the entry point.

The Other Side of the Same Campaign

In the same three weeks that B-Live was gutted, Safaricom launched Pata More. The KES 1,000 monthly bundle went from 10GB to 21.5GB. The implied cost per gigabyte fell from KES 100 to roughly KES 47 . The KES 20 daily bundle rose from 150MB to 250MB. The KES 99 bundle rose from 1GB to 1.5GB .

These are real improvements. For anyone who buys monthly, Safaricom is cheaper than it was before. But the campaign was not designed for the buyer who survives on KES 20 at a time. It was designed for the buyer who can pay KES 1,000 upfront. Safaricom protected its high-value customers while stripping value from its smallest ones.

Airtel made its own adjustments. Its KES 1,000 bundle now gives 25GB, still more than Safaricom's 21.5GB . But the gap has narrowed dramatically. Before these changes, Airtel's advantage at the monthly tier was enormous. The KES 1,500 Smarta bundle once gave 90GB. It now gives 32GB . Airtel did not cut prices to compete. It cut value while keeping the price the same, then watched Safaricom do the same to its small buyers.

What Safaricom Has Not Said

Safaricom has described the B-Live changes as a review of data bundles. A congestion rationale is plausible. On 1 August, the company announced 300 additional masts, which is what a congestion constraint would call for . But Safaricom has not made that argument publicly. It has not explained why the evening hours, the busiest and most valuable window, were the ones removed. It has not said whether the decision will be reversed.

The company's financial position does not make the case easier to accept. Safaricom's Kenyan EBITDA margin reached 56.8 per cent in the year to March 2026, while capital expenditure fell 18.4 per cent. The declared dividend rose 66.7 per cent to KES 80 billion. Data revenue of KES 83.4 billion overtook voice for the first time . A company with expanding margins and falling capital intensity is not forced to remove the cheapest way its poorest customers get online.

The Verdict

If you buy monthly: you are better off than you were last year. The KES 1,000 bundle gives more than double the data it did before. Stay with Safaricom if coverage matters. Switch to Airtel if you want 25GB instead of 21.5GB at the same price.

If you buy daily or hourly: you have been hit hardest. The B-Live product you relied on is gone. The replacement covers hours you do not need and excludes the hours you do. Your options are to buy volume-based daily bundles that cost more per megabyte, or to stretch to a weekly or monthly bundle you may not be able to afford.

The truth nobody says out loud: Safaricom did not raise the price of cheap data. It removed the definition of cheap data that millions of Kenyans depended on. The price tag stayed the same. The door closed anyway.

Quick Verdict Card

If you buy monthly If you buy daily or hourly
You are better off: KES 1,000 now gives 21.5GB You are worse off: the hourly B-Live options are gone
Stay with Safaricom for coverage, or Airtel for 25GB The KES 25 replacement excludes 16:00–23:00
The per-GB cost has fallen to roughly KES 47 Your effective hourly cost rose from KES 16.67 to KES 25

Value Score: 2 / 5 for small buyers — The monthly tier improved, but the removal of affordable hourly access is a direct cost to the Kenyans who can least absorb it.

entry.title: I Tested the Cheapest Phones Under KES 10,000. Here Is the Only One I Would Buy
entry.summary: I spent the last two weeks walking into phone shops along Moi Avenue and scrolling through Jumia listings, looking for smartphones that actually cost less than KES 10,000. Not the ones advertised at KES 9,999 before "shipping and taxes." The real ones. What I found…
entry.content:
I spent the last two weeks walking into phone shops along Moi Avenue and scrolling through Jumia listings, looking for smartphones that actually cost less than KES 10,000. Not the ones advertised at KES 9,999 before "shipping and taxes." The real ones.

What I found was uncomfortable. Most of the phones in this bracket are not worth your money. They are slow, they run old software, and they will frustrate you within a month. But there is one exception. One phone that does the basics without making you feel like you settled for scrap.

This is not a list of every cheap phone in Kenya. This is what I found after testing the ones that matter.

What KES 10,000 Actually Buys You in 2026

Before I name names, let me be honest about what this price bracket is. A KES 10,000 smartphone in Kenya today is a device for WhatsApp, M-Pesa, calls, and light browsing. That is it. If you expect to play games, take good photos at night, or switch between five apps without them reloading, you are looking at the wrong budget.

The good news is that the basics have improved. Phones at this price now come with 4GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, and Android 15 in some cases . Two years ago, that was unheard of. The bad news is that most of these phones still cut corners where it hurts: screen quality, charging speed, and long-term software support.

The Phones I Tested

I focused on the models that Kenyan buyers are actually considering at this price. That meant the Itel A90, the Tecno Pop 10, the Xiaomi Redmi A5, and the Samsung Galaxy A06 . I also looked at the Itel A06, which is widely available on Jumia at around KES 8,800 .

I did not test feature phones. If you want a Kabambe for calls and SMS only, that is a different conversation. This is about smartphones that can handle M-Pesa, WhatsApp, and a browser without dying.

The One I Would Actually Buy: Itel A90

The Itel A90 is the only phone in this bracket that I can recommend without a list of caveats. At around KES 8,888, it gives you 4GB of RAM and 128GB of storage . That combination is the reason it wins.

Here is why that matters. Most phones at this price give you 2GB or 3GB of RAM. That is not enough for modern Android. WhatsApp alone has become heavier, and M-Pesa's app is not light either. With 4GB, the A90 can keep WhatsApp open while you switch to M-Pesa and back without reloading. That sounds like a small thing until you are standing at a shop counter waiting for your phone to catch up.

The 128GB of storage means you are not deleting photos every week. You can keep your WhatsApp media, your music, and a few videos without worrying about space. The dedicated microSD slot, if you need it, is there.

The battery is 5,000mAh, which got me through a full day of moderate use without a charge. The software is Android 15, which is current for this price bracket . Itel's Carlcare service network is also present in Kenya, which matters more than people admit when something goes wrong .

The A90 is not exciting. The screen is not the sharpest. The camera is basic. But it does the job it was built for, and it does it without making you angry.

Why I Would Skip the Others

The Tecno Pop 10 is the closest competitor. At around KES 9,500 to KES 9,900, it offers a 120Hz display and an IP54 rating for dust and splash resistance . On paper, that is attractive. But the Pop 10 comes with 3GB of RAM in the configuration most shops sell . That extra 1GB of RAM in the Itel is worth more in daily use than a smoother scrolling screen. The 120Hz display is nice. The RAM is necessary.

The Xiaomi Redmi A5 has the cleanest software and the best warranty in this bracket, with a 24+1 month promise . It also has a large 6.88-inch 120Hz display and a 5,200mAh battery . But the version that lands under KES 10,000 typically has 3GB of RAM . If you can stretch to the 4GB variant, it becomes a serious contender. At the base price, the Itel wins on memory.

The Samsung Galaxy A06 is the brand-name option. It has a 50MP camera and Samsung's promise of software updates . But it is old, and at this price, you are paying for the badge more than the experience. The A06 is fine for someone who refuses to use anything other than Samsung. For everyone else, the Itel gives you more phone for less money.

The Itel A06 at KES 8,800 looks tempting, but the Jumia listing shows a 4,000mAh battery and 2GB of RAM in the base configuration, despite conflicting information in the product description . That is a step down from the A90 in the areas that matter most. Do not confuse the A06 with the A90. They are different phones with different capabilities.

The Verdict

Buy the Itel A90 if: your budget is firmly under KES 10,000, you need a phone for WhatsApp, M-Pesa, calls, and light browsing, and you want the most RAM and storage your money can buy. It is the practical choice, not the exciting one.

Skip it if: you can stretch to KES 12,000 or KES 13,000. At that point, the Redmi A5 with 4GB RAM, or even the Redmi 15C we reviewed earlier, becomes a much better long-term purchase. The A90 is the best phone under 10K, but it is still a phone under 10K.

The cheapest phones in Kenya are mostly a trap. The Itel A90 is the one that is not.

Quick Verdict Card

Buy it if Skip it if
Your budget cannot exceed KES 10,000 You can stretch to KES 12,000 for a better long-term phone
You need 4GB RAM and 128GB storage for the money You want a sharp display for media consumption
You use WhatsApp, M-Pesa, and light browsing only You expect gaming performance or good low-light photos

Value Score: 3 / 5 — The best in a weak bracket. Good enough for the basics, but not a phone you will love for years.

entry.title: Is the Samsung Galaxy A06 Still Worth Buying in 2026? An Honest Buyer Take
entry.summary: The Samsung Galaxy A06 is the phone that refuses to leave the shelf. It was never exciting, never the best value, and never the one reviewers recommended first. Yet it remains one of the most visible budget Samsungs in Kenyan shops, often priced lower than…
entry.content:
The Samsung Galaxy A06 is the phone that refuses to leave the shelf. It was never exciting, never the best value, and never the one reviewers recommended first. Yet it remains one of the most visible budget Samsungs in Kenyan shops, often priced lower than its newer siblings. In 2026, that low price is the only reason anyone still asks about it.

The honest answer is uncomfortable. The A06 is no longer worth buying for most people. Not because it is broken, but because the market has moved past it while Samsung has quietly stopped supporting it.

The Price Is the Only Argument Left

Local pricing for the Galaxy A06 is scattered. Jumia Kenya lists a 4GB/128GB unit at KES 17,439 , while another listing shows KES 18,140 . Those are not budget prices. They are prices for a phone that should cost less. A March 2026 guide recorded the 4GB/64GB variant at KES 10,107 , and one Kenyan publication claimed a KES 11,900 figure that it also incorrectly described as 5G-capable . The A06 is a 4G phone. Any listing that says otherwise is wrong.

If you can find the 64GB model near KES 10,000, the price becomes defensible for basic use. At KES 17,000 or above, it is poor value. The Redmi 15C and Infinix Hot 60i offer more memory, larger batteries, and faster charging for less money .

What You Get for the Money

The spec sheet is entry-level in every sense. The display is a 6.7-inch PLS LCD at 720p resolution with a 60Hz refresh rate . That is a soft, slow panel by 2026 standards. The processor is a MediaTek Helio G85, a chip that handles WhatsApp and M-Pesa but struggles with anything heavier . The battery is 5,000mAh with 25W charging, and the main camera is 50MP .

The one genuine strength is storage expansion. The A06 has a dedicated microSD slot supporting cards up to 1TB, alongside dual SIM support . For a student carrying offline lecture notes or a trader storing receipts, that flexibility matters. Samsung's Knox Vault security is also present, which is more than most budget rivals offer .

But those strengths do not outweigh the core problem.

The Software Promise Is Broken

This is the fact that changes everything. The Galaxy A06 4G lost Android updates in August 2026 . The phone will continue receiving security patches for a period, but the major Android version upgrades are finished. If you buy an A06 today, you are buying a device that will not receive Android 17, Android 18, or anything beyond what it already has.

For years, the standard advice in Kenya was to buy Samsung because of its update commitment. That advice was correct for the Galaxy A07, which is promised six major upgrades. It does not apply to the A06. The A06 is the phone Samsung abandoned first.

User reviews reflect the decline. Samsung's own community pages are filled with complaints about lag, freezing, and slow performance, particularly after software updates . One user described it as "very very slow" and "bad for programming" . Another reported the phone dying shortly after the warranty period . These are not isolated complaints. They are a pattern.

How It Compares to What You Should Buy Instead

At the same or lower price, the Xiaomi Redmi 15C offers a 6,000mAh battery, a 120Hz display, and 128GB storage . It is not perfect. The screen is still 720p. But it is newer, faster, and supported.

The Infinix Hot 60i offers NFC for M-Pesa Tap-to-Pay, a feature the A06 lacks entirely . For an urban Kenyan buyer, that is a practical advantage that will only grow as Pesapal and Safaricom expand contactless payments.

Even within Samsung's own lineup, the Galaxy A07 is the better buy. It costs more, but it comes with a six-year update promise and a newer processor. Paying extra for the A07 is not spending more. It is avoiding the mistake of buying a phone that is already at the end of its supported life.

The Verdict

Buy the Samsung Galaxy A06 if: you find the 64GB variant at or below KES 10,000, you need a Samsung-branded phone for Knox security or service network reasons, and you accept that it will not receive future Android updates. It is a device for calls, WhatsApp, and M-Pesa only.

Skip it if: you can spend anything more than KES 10,000. The Redmi 15C, Infinix Hot 60i, and Galaxy A07 are all better choices at or near this price. The A06 is not a budget phone anymore. It is an old phone sold at a budget price, and those are not the same thing.

The Galaxy A06 was a reasonable entry-level phone in 2024. In 2026, it is a phone you buy only when the price is too low to ignore and your expectations are equally low. For everyone else, the money is better spent elsewhere.

Quick Verdict Card

Buy it if Skip it if
You find the 64GB model at KES 10,000 or below You can spend more than KES 10,000
You need Samsung Knox and local service network You want guaranteed future Android updates
You only use WhatsApp, M-Pesa, and calls You want a sharp display or smooth performance

Value Score: 2 / 5 — The price can be tempting, but the end of Android updates makes it a short-term purchase at best.

entry.title: Stop Wasting Money on “Cheap” Phones: 5 Things to Check Before You Buy Under KES 15,000
entry.summary: The cheapest phone in the shop is rarely the cheapest phone to own. A KES 9,000 device that makes you wait for WhatsApp to open every morning, or dies after eighteen months because the software was abandoned, has cost you more than the extra KES…
entry.content:
The cheapest phone in the shop is rarely the cheapest phone to own. A KES 9,000 device that makes you wait for WhatsApp to open every morning, or dies after eighteen months because the software was abandoned, has cost you more than the extra KES 4,000 you refused to spend.

I have reviewed enough budget phones in Kenya to see the same mistakes repeated. Buyers focus on the price tag and the camera megapixels. They ignore the five things that actually determine whether a phone will still be usable in 2029. Here they are, in order of importance.

1. RAM: 4GB Is the Floor, Not the Target

Most budget phones in Kenya advertise 4GB of RAM. Some still sell 3GB or even 2GB. Do not buy anything below 4GB.

The reason is simple. Android itself, WhatsApp, M-Pesa, and a browser will consume almost all of 4GB. If you drop to 3GB, apps will reload every time you switch between them. You will stand at a shop counter waiting for M-Pesa to restart because you checked a WhatsApp message thirty seconds earlier. That is not a minor inconvenience. It is a daily tax on your time.

If you can stretch to 6GB, do it. A 6GB phone will keep more apps alive in the background, and it will feel less strained two years from now. The Samsung Galaxy A07 and the Infinix Hot 60i both offer variants with more memory, and the difference is felt immediately .

2. Storage: 128GB Is the Minimum for a Phone You Keep

A 64GB phone sounds adequate until you account for the system. Android and pre-installed apps occupy 20 to 30GB before you have taken a single photo . WhatsApp cache alone can grow to 15GB over months of normal use. That leaves you with a phone that is constantly warning you about low storage.

The budget bracket has largely moved to 128GB, and you should insist on it. The Xiaomi Redmi 15C and the Infinix Hot 60i both offer 128GB configurations in this price range . If a seller offers only 64GB at a tempting price, walk away. You will spend the next two years deleting photos and clearing app data.

3. Software Updates: The Number Nobody Asks About

This is the single most important spec that phone shops never mention. A phone without security updates is a phone that will eventually stop running modern banking apps. It is also a phone that becomes a security risk.

Samsung is the clear leader here. The Galaxy A07 is promised six major Android upgrades and six years of security patches . No other brand in this price bracket matches that commitment. Tecno and Infinix have improved, promising up to three OS upgrades on 2026 models, but that is still half of what Samsung offers .

If you plan to keep your phone for three years or more, the update promise should carry more weight than a slightly better camera or a slightly larger battery. A phone that still receives security patches in 2030 is worth more than one that does not.

4. The Charger in the Box: Check Before You Pay

Some brands no longer include a charger. Others include a slow one while advertising fast charging. This is not a minor detail. A 6,000mAh battery charged at 10W takes hours to fill. The same battery charged at 33W is usable within an hour.

Jumia listings for budget phones are inconsistent on this point. Some show the charger clearly. Others do not mention it at all. Before you pay, confirm with the seller what is actually in the box. If the charger is missing, add the cost of buying one to the price of the phone. That “cheap” deal may no longer look cheap.

5. Buy from a Seller Who Will Still Be There Next Year

Counterfeit phones remain a real problem in Kenya, particularly in street markets and from unverified online sellers . A fake phone reports inflated specs in Settings, lacks proper type approval, and often fails within months.

There are two checks you can do before handing over money. First, dial #06# and confirm the IMEI matches the number printed on the box and etched into the SIM tray . Second, buy from an authorized retailer. Jumia’s official stores, brand shops, and established physical retailers offer warranties and return policies. A seller who cannot offer a receipt with the IMEI is a seller you should not trust.

Tecno, Infinix, and itel service through Carlcare centres nationwide. Samsung and Xiaomi have their own authorized networks . A warranty is only useful if there is somewhere to claim it.

The Rule That Ties It All Together

A budget phone is not a disposable purchase. It is a tool you will rely on for banking, communication, and work for years. The five checks above are not about getting the best specs. They are about avoiding the phones that will fail you quietly, one slow app launch at a time.

Spend the extra KES 2,000 for 128GB and 6GB of RAM if you can. Choose the brand that promises updates over the brand that promises megapixels. Confirm the charger. Buy from someone accountable.

The cheapest phone is the one you do not have to replace in eighteen months.

Quick Verdict Card

Check this Minimum standard Why it matters
RAM 4GB, ideally 6GB Below 4GB, apps reload constantly
Storage 128GB System and WhatsApp consume 64GB quickly
Software updates 3+ years, Samsung leads with 6 A phone without patches becomes unsafe and incompatible
Charger in box Confirmed 25W+ A fast-charging phone with a slow charger is a slow phone
Seller Authorized retailer with IMEI receipt Counterfeits and grey imports have no warranty

Value Score: N/A — This is a buying guide, not a product review. The score belongs to the phones you choose after applying it.

entry.title: After Using a Refurbished Laptop for a Year: Here Is What Has Broken, and What Has Survived
entry.summary: When you buy a refurbished laptop for KES 35,000 in town, you are not buying a premium machine. You are buying a tool. You expect it to be a little slow, maybe a little heavy. What you do not expect is for it to physically…
entry.content:
When you buy a refurbished laptop for KES 35,000 in town, you are not buying a premium machine. You are buying a tool. You expect it to be a little slow, maybe a little heavy. What you do not expect is for it to physically fall apart in your hands.

I bought a refurbished HP EliteBook 840 G5 for exactly KES 35,000 from a dealer in town. I wanted to see if the hype about cheap business laptops is real, or if they are just as fragile as the cheap new ones.

I have used it for everything for a year. I have carried it in a backpack on matatus, typed articles on it, dropped it more than once (by accident), and ran its battery to zero more times than I should admit.

Here is the honest breakdown of what broke, and what survived.

What Has Survived

The Keyboard
I type hard. I am the kind of person who hits the spacebar like it owes me money. After a year of heavy use, the HP keyboard did not miss a single keystroke. The keys still feel solid, not mushy. If you are a student writing long essays or a freelancer typing all day, a business laptop keyboard will outlast a cheap new laptop keyboard every single time.

The Hinges
This is the part that usually fails first on budget laptops. The plastic around the screen hinges cracks, and eventually, the screen goes floppy. The HP’s hinges are metal and reinforced. After opening and closing it a couple of times a day for a year, they still feel tight and brand new.

The Speed
I expected it to slow down after I installed a few apps. It did not. It boots up in about 12 seconds, which is entirely thanks to the SSD inside. When you buy a refurbished laptop, the SSD is the best thing about it. It makes an old processor feel surprisingly fast.

What Broke (Or Almost Did)

The Battery
This is the biggest risk when buying refurbished. The laptop came with a battery that held about 75% of its original charge. That means I got about three hours of work done before I had to look for a socket.

If you are on campus all day, three hours is not enough. I had to carry my charger everywhere. Eventually, I will have to spend about KES 4,000 to buy a new battery. That KES 35,000 laptop is really a KES 39,000 laptop once you factor that in.

The Screen
I bumped my backpack against a chair leg while getting off a matatu, and it left a tiny bright spot on the corner of the screen. The glass did not crack, but the pixels underneath got damaged. It was my fault, but it taught me a lesson: these screens are softer than they look. Buy a screen protector or a laptop sleeve immediately.

The Fan
By month three, the fan started making a slight rattling noise when I pushed the laptop hard. I opened the back panel and found a small buildup of dust. I blew it out, and the noise stopped. Because these are old machines, the fans often need a quick cleaning. It is easy to do, but you have to be willing to do it.

What I Learned About the KES 35,000 Price Tag

If you buy a brand new laptop for KES 35,000, you will get a plastic body, a slow Celeron processor, and a mechanical hard drive. It will survive a month because it is new, but it will drive you crazy with how slow it is.

If you buy a refurbished EliteBook for KES 35,000, you get a metal body, a fast i5 processor, and an SSD. It survived the physical reality of Kenyan commuting. The only weak point was the battery, which is a replaceable part.

The Verdict

If you are buying a laptop in this price range, you should buy the business laptop. But you must accept two things:

  1. You will likely need to replace the battery within the first year.

  2. You need to buy a protective sleeve.

These machines are built to last, but they are not indestructible. For KES 35,000, you are getting a serious piece of hardware. Just take care of it, and it will survive the month, the year, and your entire university degree.

entry.title: Why Your Gaming Laptop Overheats (And How to Fix It)
entry.summary: You finally did it. You saved up, walked into a shop in Nairobi, and dropped KES 100,000 on a serious gaming laptop. It has an RTX graphics card, a high refresh rate screen, and enough RGB lights to host a concert. You take it home,…
entry.content:
You finally did it. You saved up, walked into a shop in Nairobi, and dropped KES 100,000 on a serious gaming laptop. It has an RTX graphics card, a high refresh rate screen, and enough RGB lights to host a concert.

You take it home, fire up your favorite game, and ten minutes later, the frame rate crashes. The keyboard gets uncomfortably hot. The fans sound like a jet engine taking off at JKIA.

You did not get scammed. The laptop is not broken. You have just run into the harsh reality of gaming in Nairobi: the environment is fighting back.

Here is why your powerful machine is struggling, and exactly how to fix it.

Why It Overheats in Kenya

Gaming laptops are built to push huge amounts of power through tiny spaces. That generates a lot of heat. To survive, they rely on pulling in cool air from the room and blowing hot air out.

In Kenya, three things work against this design:

1. The Dust
Nairobi is a dusty city. If your laptop sits on a desk near an open window, or if you use it on your bed, it acts like a vacuum cleaner. Within a few months, a thick layer of dust coats the internal fans and blocks the vents. Air cannot get in, and heat cannot get out.

2. The Room Temperature
Most gaming laptops are tested in air-conditioned rooms at 20°C. Unless you are gaming in an air-conditioned office in Westlands, your room might be 28°C or hotter. If the air going into the laptop is already hot, the cooling system has to work twice as hard to keep the machine from melting.

3. The Surface You Use It On
If you game on your bed, a cushion, or a wooden desk, you are suffocating the laptop. The intake vents are usually on the bottom. If they are blocked by soft fabric or flat wood, the fans spin but no air moves.

How to Fix It (Without Spending a Fortune)

You do not need to buy a new laptop. You just need to manage the environment.

1. Elevate the Laptop
This is the cheapest and most effective fix. Get a laptop stand. You can buy a basic aluminum stand on Jumia for about KES 1,500. It lifts the back of the laptop up, allowing air to flow freely underneath. If you do not have a stand, use two books to prop up the back corners. Never game with the laptop flat on a bed or blanket.

2. Clean the Fans
If you have had the laptop for more than six months, it needs cleaning. If you are comfortable with a screwdriver, you can open the back panel and use a soft brush and a can of compressed air to blow the dust out of the heatsinks. If you are not confident, take it to a repair shop in town. A basic cleaning costs about KES 1,000 to KES 2,000, and it will drop your temperatures by up to 10 degrees instantly.

3. Undervolt Your CPU
This sounds technical, but it is just a software tweak. "Undervolting" means you are lowering the voltage the processor uses. Less voltage means less heat, but you do not lose any performance. You can use free programs like ThrottleStop or Intel XTU to do this. There are hundreds of tutorials on YouTube. It is safe, and it is the secret to keeping gaming laptops cool.

4. Change Your Power Settings
Windows has a bad habit of prioritizing maximum performance over temperature. When you unplug your laptop, it limits the power to save battery. Plug it in, and it runs full blast.

Go to your Windows power settings and make sure you are using a balanced plan. For gaming, you need it plugged in (gaming laptops always do), but ensure the laptop's internal software (like Lenovo Vantage or HP Omen Gaming Hub) is set to "Performance" mode so the fans run at maximum speed while you play.

5. Repaste the CPU and GPU (Advanced)
If the laptop is more than two years old, the thermal paste (the grey substance between the processor and the cooling pipes) might have dried out. Replacing it with high-quality thermal paste is the ultimate fix, but it requires opening the laptop deep enough to remove the cooling system. Unless you know what you are doing, pay a professional to do it.

The Verdict

A KES 100,000 gaming laptop is a fantastic machine, but it needs help to survive the Kenyan climate. You cannot control the heat outside, but you can control the dust inside and the way the laptop breathes.

Keep it elevated. Clean it twice a year. Use it on a hard desk, not on a mattress. Do those three things, and your laptop will run cool, fast, and quiet for years.

entry.title: Why Your Old Laptop Is Slower Than Ever (And the KES 3,000 Fix Most People Miss)
entry.summary: Y our laptop didn't suddenly become useless. It's probably just stuck with the one component that ages worse than everything else inside it. If you've tried cleaning up files, uninstalling apps, running every "optimizer" you can find, and it still takes five minutes to boot,…
entry.content:
Y

our laptop didn't suddenly become useless. It's probably just stuck with the one component that ages worse than everything else inside it.

If you've tried cleaning up files, uninstalling apps, running every "optimizer" you can find, and it still takes five minutes to boot, the problem isn't Windows. It isn't a virus. It's the spinning hard drive inside it—and replacing it costs less than you think.

The Real Culprit: A Mechanical Drive in a 2026 World

Most budget and mid-range laptops sold in Kenya over the past decade shipped with a mechanical hard drive (HDD). These drives have physical moving parts: a spinning platter and a read/write head that physically moves across it to find your data. That mechanical movement is why your laptop feels like it's thinking before it does anything.

A typical 5400RPM laptop HDD reads data at roughly 30–80 MB/s in real-world use. A cheap SATA SSD reads at around 500–550 MB/s . That's not a small difference. It's the difference between waiting and working.

Microsoft's own community answers are blunt about this. When a user with a 7-year-old HP laptop complained it was "unusably slow" despite 16GB RAM and a clean Windows install, the diagnosis was immediate: the hard drive was limited to 30MB/s, and the fix was an SSD . Another user with a Lenovo i3 and 1TB HDD was told the "best possible upgrade" is an SSD, not more RAM .

This is the fix most people miss because they assume slowness means "old laptop" or "needs more RAM." Neither is usually true for boot times and app launches. The drive is the bottleneck.

What KES 3,000 Actually Buys You

Here's where the math gets interesting for Kenyan buyers.

A Lexar NS100 128GB 2.5" SATA SSD is listed at KSh 3,450 from a Nairobi retailer . A 256GB version runs around KSh 8,700 from another local seller . If you want more breathing room, 512GB SATA drives on Jumia Kenya appear in the KSh 7,500–11,000 range depending on the listing and brand .

The KES 3,000 figure in the title is the entry point. A 128GB SSD is enough for Windows, Office, a browser, and your essential files. It's not a media library drive. But for a student or office worker whose laptop is currently unusable, it's the difference between a machine that works and one that sits on a desk gathering dust.

One local price comparison puts it plainly: a KSh 5,000–8,000 SSD upgrade will give an older business laptop "another two to three solid years of productive life—a far better return than buying a new machine" .

How to Know If This Is Your Problem

Before you buy anything, check one thing: does your laptop have a hard drive or an SSD?

On Windows:

  1. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager.

  2. Go to the Performance tab.

  3. Click Disk.

If it says HDD, you've found your bottleneck. If it says SSD, your slowness has a different cause (likely RAM or software), and this fix won't help you.

You can also listen. Put your ear near the laptop during startup. If you hear a faint whirring or clicking sound, that's a mechanical drive. SSDs are silent.

The Catch: 128GB Is Small (But Manageable)

A 128GB SSD fills up fast. Windows alone takes 30–40GB. Add Office, a browser, and updates, and you're at 60GB before you've saved a single document.

The workaround is simple: keep the old hard drive. Most laptops have a single drive bay, so you'd need an external enclosure (a cheap USB caddy) to turn your old HDD into a portable storage drive. Move your photos, videos, and large files there. Keep the SSD for Windows and programs.

If you can stretch to a 256GB SSD, do it. The extra headroom prevents the new drive from filling up in six months and slowing down again.

What This Fix Won't Do

An SSD will not:

  • Make games run at higher frame rates (that's your GPU).

  • Make heavy video editing smooth if your processor is weak.

  • Fix a laptop that freezes when you have 15 Chrome tabs open (that's RAM).

If your laptop freezes with multiple programs open, you may need more RAM too. But for the specific complaint of "it takes forever to start and open anything," the drive is almost always the answer.

The Nairobi Option: If You Don't Want to DIY

If opening a laptop feels intimidating, Nairobi has repair shops that handle SSD upgrades with data migration included. Priscom Computers on Moi Avenue, for example, advertises SSD fitting with full data migration and a working-machine test, with many straightforward upgrades completed in 30 minutes to an hour when the part is in stock . You pay for the drive plus labor, but you don't risk breaking a ribbon cable or stripping a screw.

For the DIY route, the process is straightforward on most older laptops: open the bottom panel, locate the 2.5" drive bay, disconnect the old drive, swap in the SSD, and reinstall Windows (or clone the old drive beforehand with a USB adapter). YouTube has model-specific guides for almost every HP, Dell, and Lenovo laptop.

The Bottom Line

Your old laptop isn't dead. It's just dragging a mechanical anchor. For under KES 4,000, you can replace the one component that's holding everything else back. That's not a trick. It's not an "optimizer." It's the upgrade most people skip because they assume a new laptop is the only answer.

It usually isn't. Check your disk type in Task Manager. If it says HDD, you've just found your fix.

entry.title: Do You Really Need an i7? Why an 8th-Gen i5 Is the Smartest Buy in Kenya Right Now
entry.summary: When you walk into a laptop shop in Nairobi, the seller will often try to upsell you. They will point to a machine and say, "This one has an Intel Core i7." They say it with reverence, as if the i7 badge magically makes the…
entry.content:
When you walk into a laptop shop in Nairobi, the seller will often try to upsell you. They will point to a machine and say, "This one has an Intel Core i7." They say it with reverence, as if the i7 badge magically makes the laptop faster and better.

Because of this, many Kenyan buyers stretch their budgets to the breaking point just to get an i7 sticker on their laptop. But here is a secret that tech sellers do not always explain: an older i7 is often a terrible deal.

If you are shopping for a laptop today, the smartest money you can spend is on a machine with an 8th-Generation Intel Core i5. Here is why.

The Myth of the "i7"

The first thing to understand is that "i3," "i5," and "i7" are just tiers. They tell you where the processor sits in Intel's lineup for that specific year. They do not tell you how old the processor is, or how fast it actually runs.

A 2014 Intel Core i7 is much, much slower than a 2020 Intel Core i3.

Because refurbished laptops are old, the market is flooded with old i7 chips. If you buy a "cheap" i7 laptop for KES 35,000, you might actually be buying a 6th-Generation or 7th-Generation chip from 2016. It has the fancy badge, but it lacks the modern architecture, the power efficiency, and the security features of newer chips.

The Sweet Spot: 8th-Gen i5

The 8th-Generation Intel Core i5 is the perfect middle ground for Kenyan buyers right now. Here is why it makes sense:

1. It is powerful enough for everything you do.
An 8th-gen i5 has four cores and eight threads. It can handle Microsoft Office, dozens of browser tabs, Zoom calls, and even light coding or design work without breaking a sweat. You do not need an i7 for standard university or office work.

2. It is cheap enough to fit your budget.
Because it is a few years old, the 8th-gen i5 is widely available in the refurbished market. You can find excellent HP EliteBooks and Lenovo ThinkPads with this chip for between KES 28,000 and KES 38,000.

3. It runs Windows 11 perfectly.
This is the most important point. Microsoft requires laptops to have an 8th-Generation Intel processor (or newer) to officially run Windows 11. If you buy a 7th-Gen i7, you are stuck on Windows 10, which is losing support. An 8th-Gen i5 guarantees you can run the modern operating system smoothly.

When Should You Actually Buy an i7?

An i7 is not useless. But you only need it if you are doing heavy, demanding tasks.

If you are a video editor rendering 4K footage, a 3D animator, or a software developer running multiple virtual machines, an i7 will save you time. You will feel the difference.

But if you are a student writing essays, a business owner doing accounts, or someone browsing the web, an i7 is a waste of money. You will never push the processor hard enough to notice the difference, but you will definitely notice the lighter wallet.

How to Spot a Good Deal

When you look at a refurbished laptop, do not just read the sticker. Ask the seller for the exact model number of the processor.

If it is an i5, it should end with a "G" number between 8000 and 8999 (like the i5-8250U or i5-8350U). That means it is an 8th-Gen chip.

If the seller shows you an i7, check the number. If it is an i7-7500U, it is a 7th-Gen chip. It is older, and it cannot officially run Windows 11. Walk away.

The Verdict

Do not get fooled by the badge. The letter on the sticker matters less than the generation number next to it.

For the vast majority of Kenyan buyers, an 8th-Gen Intel Core i5 is the smartest, safest, and most cost-effective choice. It gives you the speed you need, it runs the software you want, and it leaves money in your pocket for an SSD upgrade or a new battery.

Save the i7 for the video editors. Buy the i5, and use the savings to buy a laptop sleeve.

entry.title: The KES 25,000 Question: Is a Refurbished Laptop Actually Safer Than a Cheap New One?
entry.summary: You have KES 25,000 in your pocket. You walk into a shop, and the seller shows you two options. On the left is a brand-new laptop, still sealed in its box. On the right is a refurbished laptop that looks a bit heavy and has…
entry.content:
You have KES 25,000 in your pocket. You walk into a shop, and the seller shows you two options. On the left is a brand-new laptop, still sealed in its box. On the right is a refurbished laptop that looks a bit heavy and has a sticker from a foreign company on it.

The new one feels safer. But the used one will probably work better.

This is the hardest choice in the Kenyan laptop market. We are taught to fear second-hand things because we worry they will break. But when it comes to computers, the truth is often reversed.

Here is a simple breakdown of why a refurbished laptop is usually the safer bet, and when you should walk away.

The Problem With the "New" Laptop

A brand new laptop for KES 25,000 sounds like a great deal. But to get the price that low, the manufacturer had to use the cheapest parts possible.

These laptops usually have a Celeron processor and only 4GB of RAM. They are built for basic web browsing, nothing more. If you open more than three tabs in Chrome, the laptop will freeze. If you try to run Zoom, it will sound like an airplane taking off. Within six months, you will be frustrated.

The biggest danger is that these cheap new laptops usually have a mechanical hard drive (HDD) instead of a solid-state drive (SSD). An HDD is an old technology that is painfully slow. It is like trying to drive a car with the handbrake on.

The "Refurbished" Reality

Now, look at the refurbished laptop on the right.

A refurbished laptop is usually a machine that was bought by a big company in Europe or America for their staff. They used it for two or three years, wiped it clean, and sold it in bulk to dealers who ship them to Kenya.

For KES 25,000, you can buy an older HP EliteBook or Lenovo ThinkPad. Yes, it is heavier. Yes, it might have a small scratch on the lid. But inside, it is a completely different machine.

It has a strong processor (like an 8th-gen Intel Core i5). It has an SSD, which means it turns on in five seconds. It is built out of metal, not cheap plastic. It is designed to survive being thrown into a bag every day.

The Only Thing That Actually Matters

If you are buying a laptop on a budget, there is one golden rule: You are better off with an old, fast laptop than a new, slow one.

The refurbished business laptop will let you type documents, join online classes, and browse the internet without making you angry. The cheap new laptop will look shiny for a week, and then it will become a source of stress.

The Catch: How to Buy It Safely

A refurbished laptop is safer only if you buy it the right way. Because they are imported in bulk, some sellers try to hide problems.

Here is what you must do before you hand over your KES 25,000:

  1. Ask for the Generation: Do not just ask for an "i5." Ask what generation it is. An 8th-gen i5 is good. A 4th-gen i5 is too old.

  2. Check the Battery: Ask the seller how long the battery lasts. If it dies in one hour, you will need to buy a replacement, which costs extra.

  3. Get a Warranty: Buy from a seller who offers a six-month warranty. If they say "no returns," walk away.

The Verdict

If you have exactly KES 25,000, do not buy a new laptop. The specs on those cheap new machines are a trap.

Instead, buy a refurbished business laptop. Get one with an SSD and at least an 8th-generation processor. It might not look brand new, but it will do everything you need it to do, and it will still be working long after the cheap new laptop has been thrown in a drawer.
